# v1.1.0-dev.66 — Resolutions, researched properly

Pre-release off the `dev` branch. Builds on `v1.1.0-dev.65`.

A research pass on how custom resolutions actually work, and the
changes it justified. Some of what it turned up was that WLM
should do less, not more.

## Your Portrait Monitor Had No Grouping

The resolution list groups sizes by shape: 16:9 together, 21:9
together, and so on. On a rotated display every single size landed
in one bucket called "Portrait". A long list stayed a long flat list
exactly where the grouping was most useful.

A 16:9 panel stood on its end is still 16:9. It's grouped that way
now and labelled **16:9 (portrait)**.

While in there: 5:4 is a real shape and is in the table now. A group
with only one size in it folds into "Other shapes" rather than
printing a heading with a single row underneath.

## "Test" Was Not A Test

The button called **Test** applied the change to your displays
permanently. There was no undo.

Every comparable tool has an escape hatch. Windows gives you fifteen
seconds of Keep or Revert. NVIDIA makes you confirm after a test.
macOS counts down. CRU watches for F8. WLM had none of that. The
word "Test" was promising something that did not exist.

It's called **Apply now**. The tooltip says plainly that there is no
undo. A real fifteen-second revert is the better answer, written
down as still to do.

## "Show Every Size" Sounded Dangerous

NVIDIA has a checkbox called "enable resolutions not exposed by the
display". It carries a hardware warning, because it does something
genuinely risky.

WLM's checkbox read almost the same and does nothing of the sort.
It only unhides small sizes your driver already offers. It says
**Include small sizes**.

## Registering A Resolution Checks It First

WLM would accept anything from 640×480 to 16384×16384 at up to
1000 Hz. Parsec's driver actually offers 1280×720 up to 4096×2160
at up to 240 Hz. Those bounds were about four times too generous on
every axis.

That mattered because Parsec only gives WLM two slots. You could
spend an administrator prompt and one of your two slots on a size
the driver was never going to offer, and find out after a session
reconnect.

Sizes are now checked against the driver's own declared range
before the prompt appears. The message names the driver:

```
7680 × 4320 @ 60 Hz is outside what this driver offers.
Parsec tops out at 4096 pixels wide.
```

Windows would not have refused that. WLM refuses it on the driver's
behalf, which is why it says whose limit it is.

## What The Research Argued Against

Worth listing, because these all sounded like good ideas:

**No pixel clock or timing validation.** A virtual display's mode
carries no timing information at all. There is nothing to compute.
A clock check would reject valid sizes while passing invalid ones.

**No multiple-of-8 rule and no aspect-ratio check.** Both are
encoding artefacts rather than hardware requirements. Both would
reject sizes drivers already ship.

**No reading a virtual display's EDID for a ceiling.** Parsec's
advertises 1920×1080 and 165 Hz while its driver offers 4096×2160
at 240 Hz. Trusting it would cap you at under half the real range.

## Also

The Virtual Display Driver hint was wrong. One binary reads both
config files, `vdd_settings.xml` first with `option.txt` as a
fallback, split at release 24.8.6. WLM described it as one or the
other depending on build.

## Still Open

A tool called ParsecDisplay compacts the resolution slots when it
reads them. On a machine where Parsec owns slots 2 to 4 and yours
are empty, one press of its Apply button shuffles Parsec's own
resolutions down into the slots WLM treats as yours. Slot position
turns out not to prove ownership. That needs a real fix and does
not have one yet.

The registry slots missing on the machine that reported the
original bug are still unexplained. Registration now reads the key
back and reports what it actually finds. A silent failure will at
least announce itself.

## Install

Auto-updates from dev.53 and later. Otherwise unzip and run.
